title: The Slow Making of Dispositions
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Boymal starts from the Australian Treasury's 2026 Intergenerational Report, which says judgement, coordination, accountability, tacit knowledge and relationships will keep their value as AI automates tasks. He treats these as dispositions and asks how thinkers across cultures say they are formed. The unifying idea is Bildung, the lifelong shaping of a whole person, which he traces from Humboldt, Goethe and Gadamer through Aristotle, Wang Yangming, Murdoch, Weil, Polanyi, Sennett, Smith, Arendt, Confucius, Ostrom, Buber and Yunkaporta. Judgement grows from habit and attention, tacit knowledge from practice in company, accountability from being seen, coordination from rehearsed courtesy and trust, and character from relationships. The practical sting is a pipeline problem: the junior tasks AI absorbs most readily are exactly where novices have always learned. He closes by urging universities, firms and professions to protect the places where novices work beside experts on real problems with real stakes.
points: Boymal frames the Treasury's list of human strengths as dispositions that are acquired slowly through practice, company, stakes and time rather than taught as information.
Aristotle's habituation, Murdoch's attention and Weil's schoolwork-as-attention together show that moral and practical judgement is trained long before any decision is made.
Tacit knowledge, from Polanyi to Sennett and Lave and Wenger, is passed on by working alongside experts, which is why legitimate peripheral participation matters.
AI absorbs junior tasks first, so it risks thinning the apprenticeship pipeline that produces senior judgement, a concern Boymal links to Becker's human capital analysis.
His prescription is institutional: protect mentoring, early-career roles and assessment designs where people still decide, explain and answer for their choices.
quotes: Bildung means the lifelong shaping of a whole person, in which knowledge, character and perception develop together.
Aristotle’s example is the experienced physician, who knows what to do for this patient, a knowledge that comes from many patients.
Murdoch’s claim is that the moral work took place in the looking, and that most of our ethical life happens in the quality of our attention before any choice arises.
The ballad describes a person who holds a powerful instrument without the formation that makes its use safe. Any technology that offers capability ahead of competence invites the same scene.
A trainee who never signs anything, never defends a choice to a sceptical colleague and never lives with an error has nothing for the inner spectator to build on.
The dispositions need practice, because they are habits. They need company, because mentors, colleagues and communities carry what cannot be written down.
A society that wants judgement, trust and accountability in its workforce will want to keep that soil rich.
